subject: Connectivity choice for Cobalt Systems: peering vs PrivateLink vs S2S VPN
messages:

Subject: Connectivity options for Redwood private deployment

Marissa,

Thanks for taking this on. A quick summary of our environment and constraints so you can tailor recommendations:
- We have a dedicated VPC in us-west-2 with a handful of accounts for our infra.
- Sensitive PHI data is stored on-prem in our Azure data center (east-us), and we need HIPAA-safe transport and auditability.
- Some inference endpoints need sub-50ms RTT to on-prem systems for real-time lookups (~50 RPS typical, spikes to 200).
- Cost sensitivity: we run a lot of tokens; we'd like to keep egress/ingress networking costs reasonable.

Primary question: for Redwood Private (VPC + on-prem) what's your recommendation between VPC peering, PrivateLink, and site-to-site VPN? We care about security boundaries, operational complexity, failover behavior, and how each option affects latency/cost.

Also if you can include an estimate of lead time / pilot approach and any constraints about cross-account peering or multi-region patterns, that would be great.

I've attached our short network inventory and a quick diagram.

[Attachment: cobalt_datacenter_diagram.png (image/png)]

Appreciate a pragmatic recommendation we can take to our infra team.

— Alex

Subject: RE: Connectivity options for Redwood private deployment

Alex — thanks for the clear summary. Looping in Ben (solutions lead), Karthik (infra / networking), and Lauren (security & compliance) so we can give a concise recommendation and an executable pilot plan.

High-level guidance up front (short version):
- PrivateLink for control-plane and management API traffic where you need strict per-account isolation and no cross-account routing; PrivateLink keeps endpoints in your VPC and avoids complex peering ACLs.
- S2S VPN as the pragmatic data-plane option for encrypted, auditable tunnels to your on-prem site (fast to stand up, supports strong enc ciphers, good for initial pilot).
- If sub-50ms latency is mandatory for all traffic, evaluate a Direct Connect / ExpressRoute equivalent (dedicated private circuit) or colocated edge if budget allows; VPC peering alone won't cross cloud-provider boundaries and has cross-account constraints.

I've attached a comparison matrix and a preliminary architecture diagram. Next steps I propose: quick 45-minute alignment call early next week to validate constraints, then a short pilot SOW (2 weeks: connectivity + smoke tests + latency measurements).

Action items for us:
- Karthik: fill in operational steps and firewall requirements.
- Ben: provide pricing delta estimates for VPN vs PrivateLink vs Direct Connect.
- Lauren: confirm logging/audit control expectations (HIPAA / SOC2) and call out any gaps.

Attachments: cobalt_connectivity_matrix_v2.xlsx, redwood_private_arch_diag_v1.png

Thanks — talk soon.

Subject: Re: Connectivity options for Redwood private deployment — technical notes

Marissa / team — quick technical rundown and configuration sketch. Quoting Alex's constraints above for context.

Key constraints recapped: cross-cloud on-prem (Azure), sub-50ms target for some flows, HIPAA encryption + audit, 50–200 RPS inference spikes.

Recommendations (technical):
1) Control / Management plane: AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoints)
   - Pros: no routing into Redwood networks, strong per-service access control, easier to audit (interface endpoints + flow logs), lower blast radius.
   - Cons: cost per ENI/endpoint and data processed; needs endpoint services in the model-serving account or a GW endpoint pattern.

2) Data plane (inference traffic) — staged approach:
   - Pilot: IPSec S2S VPN between Cobalt on-prem and Redwood VPCs (terminates at a virtual appliance / TGW).
     - Pros: fast to deploy, fully encrypted, supports BGP for path failover, easy to test with smoke traffic.
     - Cons: potentially higher latency and egress costs across cloud provider interconnects; MTU/pktsize tuning may be needed for model payloads.
   - Production-scale (if latency & throughput justify): Azure ExpressRoute + AWS Direct Connect interconnect or a colocated interconnect via a partner (megaport / equinix).
     - Pros: predictable latency, lower variable egress costs, better SLAs.
     - Cons: setup lead time (4–8 weeks), cross-provider circuit ops.

3) VPC Peering:
   - Useful for same-cloud, same-account low-latency connections between Redwood-managed accounts.
   - Not suitable for cross-cloud on-prem access and scales poorly when many accounts require transitive routing.

Operational notes / firewall rules:
- We should recommend CIDR ACL templates and allow lists for the specific subnet ranges used by the inference nodes.
- Turn on VPC Flow Logs + PrivateLink ENI flow logs + centralized s3 for logs (retention configurable) to meet HIPAA audit requirements.
- For S2S: require AES-256-GCM / IKEv2, SHA2, use PFS, and ensure key rotation SLA in SOW.

Cost drivers to budget for: data egress (cloud to cloud / on-prem), PrivateLink per-GB charges, VPN gateway-hours and appliance cost if using third-party virtual appliances, and one-time Direct Connect/ExpressRoute porting.

I'll spell these out into a short tech appendix that we can attach to the SOW draft.

— Karthik

Subject: RE: Connectivity options for Redwood private deployment — next steps and SOW

Alex — great questions. Quick answers and next steps below.

1) PrivateLink + logging: yes — PrivateLink interface ENIs generate VPC Flow Logs and we can emit endpoint-specific metrics + request logs to a centralized bucket (we include an audit-friendly manifest in the SOW). We'll have our security team (Lauren) complete the vendor questionnaire by EOD Wednesday.

2) VPN termination recommendation: for the pilot, terminate to a virtual appliance (Palo Alto NGFW / FortiGate) in the AWS account that holds the TGW to give you familiar firewall controls and deep packet inspection for HIPAA auditing. For production, if you prioritize latency/throughput, we can propose an ExpressRoute + Direct Connect circuit and terminate at a colo with a partner.

3) Pilot duration & SLA measurement: we typically run a 10-business-day pilot to capture steady-state and spike behaviors (includes baseline, two synthetic spike days, and failover tests). That gives us enough samples to estimate P50/P95 latency and token-volume egress.

I've attached a short SOW draft (sow-draft-cobalt.docx) that includes: scope (pilot + smoke tests), responsibilities, expected deliverables (connectivity matrix filled, latency report, recommended production path), and a pricing placeholder. Review and we can turn it into a signed SOW.

Proposed next meeting: Thu Jul 1 2027 10:00 AM PT — 30 minutes to confirm pilot scope. Does that work for your team?

Thanks — I’ll track the questionnaire and the SOW updates.

Best,
